solutions.title: Compute
solutions.body:
$\frac{2-1}2=\frac12$ and $2^{-1}\cdot\frac{2}{1}=1$, so the expression is $\frac12\cdot(1+1)=1$ (this is $S_1$).

**Answer: 1**

prompt: Notation: $\sum_{i=a}^bk_i$ is the sum and $\prod_{i=a}^bk_i$ the product of the numbers $k_i$ for $i$ from $a$ to $b$. For $n\ge1$ let $$S_n=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{2^i-1}{2^i}\right)\cdot\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^n\left(2^{-i}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^i\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}\right)\right).$$ Find a recurrence relation, writing $S_{n+1}$ in terms of $S_n$.

solutions.title: Split off the last term
solutions.body:
Write $\Pi_n=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{2^i-1}{2^i}$ and $\Sigma_n=1+\sum_{i=1}^n2^{-i}\prod_{j=1}^i\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}$, so $S_n=\Pi_n\Sigma_n$. Then $\Pi_{n+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^{n+1}}\Pi_n$ and $\Sigma_{n+1}=\Sigma_n+2^{-(n+1)}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}$. So $$S_{n+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^{n+1}}\Pi_n\Sigma_n+\Pi_{n+1}\cdot2^{-(n+1)}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}.$$ The last product $\Pi_{n+1}\prod_{j=1}^{n+1}\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}$ equals $1$ (the factors cancel), so $$S_{n+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^{n+1}}S_n+2^{-(n+1)}.$$

**Answer: $S_{n+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^{n+1}}S_n+2^{-n-1}$**

prompt: Notation: $\sum_{i=a}^bk_i$ is the sum and $\prod_{i=a}^bk_i$ the product of the numbers $k_i$ for $i$ from $a$ to $b$. For $n\ge1$ let $$S_n=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{2^i-1}{2^i}\right)\cdot\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^n\left(2^{-i}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^i\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}\right)\right).$$ Given that $\prod_{i=1}^\infty\frac{2^i-1}{2^i}\ne0$, show by induction that $$\left(\prod_{i=1}^\infty\frac{2^i-1}{2^i}\right)\cdot\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^\infty\left(2^{-i}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^i\frac{2^j}{2^j-1}\right)\right)=1.$$ (You may use the recurrence $S_{n+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^{n+1}}S_n+2^{-(n+1)}$.)
answer: The infinite product times the infinite bracket equals 1 (proof)

solutions.title: Induction and limit
solutions.body: Claim: $S_n=1$ for all $n\ge1$. Base: $S_1=1$ (computed directly: $\frac12(1+1)=1$). Step: if $S_n=1$ then $S_{n+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{2^{n+1}}+2^{-(n+1)}=1$. So $S_n=1$ for all $n$. As $n\to\infty$, $\Pi_n\to\Pi_\infty\ne0$ and $\Pi_n\Sigma_n=1$, so $\Sigma_n=\frac1{\Pi_n}\to\frac1{\Pi_\infty}$, which means the series converges and $\Pi_\infty\Sigma_\infty=\lim\Pi_n\Sigma_n=1$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Define $\binom nk$ as the number of ways to choose $k$ things out of $n$ choices. Give a combinatorial proof (without any algebra) that $$\binom nk=\binom{n-1}k+\binom{n-1}{k-1}.$$ (A combinatorial proof counts the same quantity in two ways.)
answer: Count $k$-subsets of an $n$-set by whether they contain a fixed element

solutions.title: Double counting
solutions.body: Let $X$ be a set with $n$ elements and fix one element $x\in X$. The $k$-element subsets of $X$ number $\binom nk$. Split them into those that do not contain $x$, which are $k$-subsets of the other $n-1$ elements ($\binom{n-1}k$ of them), and those that contain $x$, which correspond to choosing the remaining $k-1$ elements from the other $n-1$ ($\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ of them). Every $k$-subset is in exactly one class, so $\binom nk=\binom{n-1}k+\binom{n-1}{k-1}$. $\blacksquare$
